listeningScripts.title: Arranging a Water Meter
listeningScripts.text:
Advisor: Good afternoon, Ravensmere Water, customer services.
Caller: Hello — I'd like to ask about having a water meter fitted.
Advisor: Certainly. Can I take your name?
Caller: It's Aurelia Bankole. Bankole is B-A-N-K-O-L-E.
Advisor: And the property address?
Caller: Thirty-one Coppice Lane.
Advisor: Thank you. How many people live there?
Caller: Just me and my daughter.
Advisor: Then a meter will almost certainly save you money. The general rule is that if there are fewer people than bedrooms, metering is cheaper — and it's worth knowing you can switch back within two years if it isn't.
Caller: I didn't know that. Is there a charge for fitting?
Advisor: No charge for the meter or the installation. What I would flag is that if the pipework needs altering to reach the stop tap, that part isn't covered, and it's typically ninety pounds.
Caller: How would I know if that applies?
Advisor: The engineer assesses it on the day and tells you before doing anything.
Caller: Fine. How long does fitting take?
Advisor: Usually about an hour. The water is off for roughly twenty minutes of that.
Caller: When could someone come?
Advisor: I have the sixth of May or the twentieth.
Caller: The sixth, please. Morning or afternoon?
Advisor: Morning slots are eight to twelve, afternoons twelve to four.
Caller: Afternoon, please.
Advisor: Booked. Somebody over eighteen needs to be there, and the engineer needs access to the stop tap — which is usually under the kitchen sink, so please clear the cupboard beforehand. That one request saves more failed appointments than anything else we ask.
Caller: I'll do that. When would the first metered bill come?
Advisor: We read it after six months, and until then you keep paying the old rate. The first metered bill is therefore about seven months away, and any difference is adjusted then rather than backdated.

listeningScripts.title: Community Radio Induction
listeningScripts.text:
Manager: Evening, everyone, and welcome to Bridgehead Community Radio. I'm Femi, the station manager, and this is the induction for new volunteers.

Let me start with what we are, because it affects everything. We are a community station, not a small commercial one. That means our licence obliges us to serve this area specifically, and it means we cannot simply play whatever we like — a set proportion of our output has to be speech, locally made, and about this place. If you want to present a music show that could come from anywhere, this is the wrong station, and I would rather say that now than in six weeks.

Training is in three stages. Everyone does the studio session, which is two hours and covers the desk. Then you shadow an existing presenter for at least four programmes — not two, four, and people always ask. Only then do you go live, and your first three programmes are pre-recorded rather than broadcast as they happen.

The rules that will end your involvement if broken are short and I will state them plainly. Nothing goes out that you have not cleared for language or for defamation. No political opinion in your own voice during an election period. And no dead air longer than about thirty seconds, which sounds trivial and is what listeners notice above everything else.

The building. Coming in the front door, the office is immediately on your left, and that's where the rota lives. Studio One, which is the on-air studio, is straight ahead through the double doors at the end of the corridor. Studio Two, used for recording and editing, is beside it on the right of the corridor. The kitchen is opposite Studio Two, on the left. And the record library, which is still worth using, is upstairs above the office.

Last thing. If something goes wrong on air — and it will — say what has happened in plain words and carry on. Listeners forgive mistakes instantly and forgive pretending nothing happened rather more slowly.

listeningScripts.title: Planning a Dissertation Timetable
listeningScripts.text:
Supervisor: Right, let's put a timetable on this dissertation. When is it due?
Ravi: The fourteenth of September.
Supervisor: And today is the twentieth of March, so you have just under six months. How are you planning to divide that?
Ravi: I thought three months reading, two months writing, then a month to tidy up.
Supervisor: That is the plan almost everyone brings me and it fails in the same way each time. What happens in month five?
Ravi: I'd be writing.
Supervisor: You would be discovering that a chapter needs a source you have not read, and going back into reading with no time left for it. Reading and writing are not sequential activities.
Ravi: So how should I split it?
Supervisor: Write from the start. Produce something written every week from now — even badly — because writing is how you find out what you do not yet know. The reading then has a purpose beyond accumulation.
Ravi: What about the data collection?
Supervisor: When does that have to happen?
Ravi: The interviews need to be in June, because that's when the participants are available.
Supervisor: Then June is fixed and everything else moves around it. Work backwards: transcription in July, analysis in July and August, and a complete draft — bad but complete — by the middle of August.
Ravi: A month before the deadline?
Supervisor: Yes, and that month is not spare. It is for the things nobody plans for: a chapter that has to be rewritten, an ethics form you forgot, a printer that fails, an illness. Students who finish comfortably are not faster writers; they had a complete draft early.
Ravi: What should I send you, and when?
Supervisor: A chapter at a time, and do not wait until one is good. I can be far more useful on a rough chapter in April than on a polished one in September.

listeningScripts.title: Why Disaster Losses Rise
listeningScripts.text:
Lecturer: The economic losses from weather-related disasters have risen substantially over recent decades. That figure is frequently quoted as evidence of how much more severe such events have become, and today I want to look at why the inference does not follow from that number alone.

The reason is exposure. There are more people and far more property in the places these events strike than there were fifty years ago — coasts have been developed, cities have expanded onto floodplains, and the value of what stands in any given hectare has risen enormously. An identical storm hitting an identical coastline today destroys more because there is more there to destroy.

When researchers correct for that — by asking what a past event would cost if it struck today's built environment, which is called normalising the record — the strong upward trend in most loss series weakens considerably, and in several categories disappears. That is a real finding and it is routinely misused, so let me be careful about what it does and does not show.

It does not show that the climate signal is absent. It shows that losses are a poor instrument for detecting it, because the exposure term is large, fast-growing, and swamps whatever change is occurring in the hazard itself. To detect a change in the hazard you have to measure the hazard — rainfall intensity, wind speed, sea temperature — rather than the cost of the damage.

And when you do measure the hazard directly, the picture is not uniform, which is the part both sides of the public argument tend to skip. The evidence for increases is strong for heat extremes and for heavy rainfall, moderate and improving for drought in certain regions, and genuinely weak for some other categories where the physical reasoning is less direct and the record is short.

The practical implication points somewhere unexpected. Since exposure explains most of the rise in losses, the most reliable way to reduce future losses is to act on exposure — where building is permitted, to what standard, and whether the people who benefit from building in a hazardous place bear the cost of doing so. That conclusion holds whatever the hazard trend turns out to be, which makes it the rare recommendation that does not depend on winning the argument first.
